newsitem.title: USA: Firebrand Louisiana legislator may win Senate race.
newsitem.headline: Firebrand Louisiana legislator may win Senate race.

text.p: Woody Jenkins, a feisty anti-tax, anti-abortion legislator who has annoyed Louisiana governors for 24 years, could become on Tuesday the state's first Republican U.S. senator this century, analysts said.
Heading for election day with Jenkins in a dead heat with former Democratic state Treasurer Mary Landrieu, 40, analysts said the Nov. 5 election was too close to call.
"This is the first real two-party U.S. Senate race in Louisiana this century and it's a toss-up," Louisiana State University political science professor Wayne Parent said.

Since taking office as a state representative in 1972, Jenkins, 49, has been known for his strongly held beliefs on issues ranging from gun control to property rights. He drew national attention in 1990 and 1991 by waving a plastic foetus during a campaign to ban abortions in Louisiana, with saving a mother's life as the only exception.
His uncompromising stand often annoyed other abortion foes who were willing to grant exceptions for rape or incest.

"There was just no moving him to get even most of what we wanted," said one irritated anti-abortion crusader who is now actively campaigning for Jenkins for Senate. "But at least I guess we won't have to worry about him giving away the farm in Washington."

During his earlier legislative years, Jenkins took the podium on almost every issue. In recent years, he has focused on touchy issues such as greater freedom from government intervention in private academies and home schooling, gun control and limits on intrusive police powers.

The only thing he has switched is his party affiliation: from Republican to Democrat in 1970 and back to Republican in 1994 after he gave up trying to push the Democratic Party toward the political right.

The Baton Rouge native has been a founding member and active participant in several national conservative groups, including the Council for National Policy. He was the group's executive director for four years.
In the mid-1980s, Jenkins and his wife Diane founded Friends of the Americas to provide disaster relief and medical care in Latin America, which now has a $1.5 million budget and 70 employees.
He has denied allegations that he and his family profited excessively from the charity and more recent charges that the charity was tied to wrongdoing in the Iran-contra scandal.
Jenkins favours abolishing the Internal Revenue Service and replacing the income tax with a national sales tax.

He grew up in a blue-collar Baton Rouge neighbourhood, son of a disabled World War II veteran. While working to help support his family, Jenkins majored in journalism at Louisiana State University before earning a law degree.
He is married to his high school sweetheart Diane Jenkins. The couple have four children.
